learnerStatement: Simulated learner. This review finds problems; it is not evidence that anyone learned.
learnerBoundary: Everyday numeracy, simple charts, comparing numbers and familiar household objects; no domain-specific theory assumed.

observations.prediction: Selected one in four and locked the joint white-and-wrinkled fraction for two parents carrying one hidden copy of each independently inherited form.
observations.exploration: Crossed the parents to fill sixteen equally likely combinations. Marked white: four of sixteen. Marked wrinkled: four of sixteen. Marked both: one of sixteen.
observations.reveal: The reveal corrected the answer to one in sixteen and explained a quarter of the white seeds are wrinkled because the genes are inherited separately. It gave one quarter times one quarter and qualified the rule with linked genes on a chromosome.
observations.visual: Inspected the inline dark 1257 by 936 screenshot with white highlighted. A four by four grid encoded flower color by fill and seed shape by outline; four white cells were outlined green. Row and column symbols and a legend supported interpreting the combinations.
observations.isolation: No-history evaluation preview banner present. Visible trust count ignored.
observations.reference: Own CUA tab 543884163 snapshots and inspected inline screenshot; no screenshot file saved.

prediction.reason: The question distinguishes a single recessive fraction from the joint event.
prediction.evidence: Selected one in four before seeing the joint overlap.

interaction.reason: Single-trait filters and a joint filter expose the probability intersection.
interaction.evidence: Both individual filters select four cells, but the joint filter selects one.

payoff.reason: The reveal explains multiplication and explicitly states the independence limit.
payoff.evidence: It gives 1/4 times 1/4 and notes nearby linked genes can break the rule.

clarity.reason: Color and shape provide two separable encodings with explicit counts.
clarity.evidence: The grid and legend distinguish white fill from wrinkled outline.

transfer.reason: The independent chance rule is stated without a new genetics cross or other application.
transfer.evidence: Only this fixed two-trait example is available.

accessibility.evidence: Keyboard, focus, contrast audit, phone, zoom/reflow and motion unknown.

surprise.reason: Combining two hidden traits is much rarer than either alone.
surprise.evidence: Four selected cells for each single trait reduce to one joint cell.

visualExplanation.reason: Filtering the common grid makes the overlap visible.
visualExplanation.evidence: All three counts refer to the same sixteen combinations.

playfulness.reason: Crossing and filtering supports a guided discovery.
playfulness.evidence: Four controls fill and highlight a fixed grid.

practicalValue.reason: It connects independent inheritance to multiplication of chances.
practicalValue.evidence: The reveal includes the important independence condition.

depth.reason: The lesson explains the joint fraction and a biological boundary.
depth.evidence: Linked genes are named as a reason the simple multiplication can fail.

complexity.reason: The fraction comparison is simple, but hidden copies, gametes and independent inheritance are unfamiliar.
complexity.conceptualDemand: Moderate: distinguish individual trait chances from their joint occurrence.
complexity.interfaceBurden: Low: cross button and three filters.
complexity.conceptualChallenge: Combine two separately inherited recessive requirements.
complexity.prerequisiteNovelty: Recessive inheritance and chromosome linkage are introduced.
complexity.notationRepresentationBurden: Moderate: four by four crossing grid, dual visual encoding and fraction multiplication.

whyCool: Two separate one-in-four patterns share only one cell when both conditions must hold.
caveat: The plant and inheritance setup are invented and fixed; linkage is mentioned but not demonstrated.
missingEvidence: No fresh parent genotypes or linked-gene case was tested.
